title: Explaining how
job: Steps and instructions in order, and what they are for
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The imperative is a FORMATION, not a word to memorise: take the you-form of the present, drop the ta-, and if what is left begins with two consonants put a helping vowel in front of it. taftaḥ → ftaḥ → iftaḥ; taktub → ktub → uktub, the helper copying the stem's u. Where the remainder already begins with a single consonant nothing is added: taḍaʿ → ḍaʿ.
Three endings on one stem: iftaḥ to a man, iftaḥī to a woman, iftaḥū to a group. They are the same -ī and -ū the present tense already uses, so the only new thing is where they go.

The rule is mechanical, not universal. khudh (L2-M4) and kul (L2-M1) come out shorter than it predicts, and a longer verb needs no helping vowel at all: sāʿid, tafaḍḍal, aʿṭi. The six imperatives the ladder handed you as words stay words; the rule is for the verbs you already own in the present.

li- on the front of a verb is PURPOSE: iftaḥ al-bāb li-yadkhul al-hawāʾ. It is the same letter as L1-M9's li-ʾanna, and the two jobs sit beside each other — li-ʾanna answers why it happened, li- + verb answers what it is for. kay and min ajl an are its twins and are not opened here.

English says an infinitive of purpose: open it TO let the air in. Arabic has no infinitive to put there — the verb after li- carries a person, so li-yadkhul is "so that IT comes in" and li-aftaḥ is "so that I open". Choosing the wrong person is the mistake this module plates.

The verb after li- is in the SUBJUNCTIVE, and this course writes no mood endings, so on the page it is spelled exactly like the ordinary present — L3-M2 rule 3 flagged the mood as L4's and L3-M4 rule 4 already spelled a jussive this way. What is new here is the connector, not a verb shape.

Arabic has no negative imperative at all. A prohibition is lā in front of the you-form of the present — lā tadhhab, taught in L3-M4 rule 5 and only re-used here — so the shape it borrows is the very one the positive imperative was made by throwing away.

The step spine is awwalan … thāniyan … thumma … baʿda dhālika … akhīran, and it lands where English lands it. Only thāniyan is bought here: awwalan, akhīran and baʿda dhālika are L3-M1's and thumma is L1-M10's.

words.note: taftaḥ minus its ta- leaves ftaḥ, which cannot open a word, so a helping i- goes in front: iftaḥ. Add -ī to a woman, -ū to a group.

sentences.trap: English has one imperative for everybody. Arabic picks its ending from who is being addressed, so "open" is already three words before anything else has been said.
sentences.sound: if-TAḤ — the i- is a run-up rather than a syllable you lean on, and the final ḥ is the breathy one from deep in the throat, not an h.

variations.cue: First, open the book
variations.changed: the thing opened: al-bāb → al-kitāb

variations.cue: First, open the door (to a woman)
variations.changed: who is being told: the -ī ending

mistake.why: That is the ordinary present — "first, you open the door" — a description of what happens rather than an instruction. The ta- has to come off before it is an order.

sentences.usage: The opening move of any set of directions: a recipe, a form, a machine, a route.
sentences.mnemonic: Drop the ta-, and if the rest trips over itself, slide a vowel under it.

sentences.cue: Open the window so the air comes in

words.note: li- on a verb is purpose. The same letter as L1-M9's li-ʾanna: li-ʾanna answers why it happened, li- + verb answers what it is for.
Feminine, like most nouns ending in -a. n is a sun letter, so the article's l is swallowed and it is heard an-nāfidha.
Ends in hamza, written ʾ — the catch in the throat. It is not the ʿayn of ʿamal, and the two are never swapped.

sentences.trap: English puts an infinitive after "to": to let the air in. Arabic has none to put there, so the verb behind li- carries a person — li-yadkhul is literally "so that IT comes in".
sentences.sound: li-YAD-khul runs as one word with no pause after the li-, and the final -ʾ of hawāʾ is a stop, not a vowel trailing away.

variations.cue: Open the door so the air comes in
variations.changed: what is opened: an-nāfidha → al-bāb

variations.cue: Open the window, all of you, so the air comes in
variations.changed: who is being told: the plural -ū

mistake.why: li-adkhul is "so that I come in". The person on the verb after li- has to be whoever does the entering — here the air — so it is li-yadkhul.

sentences.usage: How a reason gets attached to an instruction: do this, and here is what it is for.
sentences.mnemonic: li- plus a verb answers what for — and the verb still has to say who.

sentences.display: ḍaʿ as-sukkar fī al-qahwa, thumma ishrab
sentences.script: ضع السكر في القهوة، ثم اشرب
sentences.cue: Put the sugar in the coffee, then drink
sentences.literal: Put the-sugar in the-coffee, then drink

words.note: taḍaʿ minus ta- leaves ḍaʿ, which already begins with a single consonant, so no helping vowel is added. The shortest imperatives are the ones needing no help.
s is a sun letter: the article's l is swallowed by it, so al-sukkar is said and written as-sukkar.

sentences.trap: ishrab arrived in L2-M1 as a word to be memorised. It was a derivation all along — tashrab minus its ta-, with a helping i- in front — and nothing about it was special.
sentences.sound: ḍaʿ is one heavy syllable: the ḍ is the emphatic d, made with the tongue flat, and the ʿ closes it in the throat.

variations.display: ḍaʿ al-māʾ fī al-qahwa, thumma ishrab
variations.script: ضع الماء في القهوة، ثم اشرب
variations.cue: Put the water in the coffee, then drink
variations.changed: what is put in: as-sukkar → al-māʾ

variations.display: ḍaʿ al-khubz ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila, thumma kul
variations.script: ضع الخبز على الطاولة، ثم كل
variations.cue: Put the bread on the table, then eat
variations.changed: both steps, kept in the same frame

mistake.display: taḍaʿ as-sukkar fī al-qahwa, thumma tashrab
mistake.script: تضع السكر في القهوة، ثم تشرب
mistake.why: Both verbs still wear their ta-, so this reports what someone does instead of telling them to do it. A recipe in Arabic is imperatives all the way down.

sentences.usage: The shape of every recipe step and every set of instructions handed over a counter.
sentences.mnemonic: ḍaʿ needs no run-up — one consonant in front is enough to stand on.

sentences.display: idhhabū ilā as-sūq, wa khudhū al-khubz
sentences.cue: Go to the market, all of you, and take the bread
sentences.literal: Go(pl) to the-market, and take(pl) the-bread

words.note: The plural of L2-M4's idhhab, with -ū on the end. A plural imperative is a different surface from its singular, so it gets a row of its own here.
The plural of L2-M4's khudh. khudh is one of the two verbs shorter than the rule predicts, and the plural ending goes onto it unchanged.

sentences.trap: English says "go" to one person and to twenty. Arabic changes the word, and a singular aimed at a group is heard by everyone in it.
sentences.sound: idh-ha-BŪ — the dh is the one in "this", and the long ū at the end carries the stress.

variations.display: idhhabū ilā al-bayt, wa khudhū al-māʾ
variations.cue: Go home, all of you, and take the water
variations.changed: where and what: as-sūq → al-bayt, al-khubz → al-māʾ

variations.display: idhhab ilā as-sūq, wa khudh al-khubz
variations.cue: Go to the market and take the bread
variations.changed: the addressee: one man instead of a group

mistake.why: The prefix is still there, so this is "you (pl.) go" — a statement. Take the ta- off and the plural ending stays exactly where it was: idhhabū.

sentences.usage: What a guide, a teacher or a parent says to a room. The singular in the same situation sounds like you are picking somebody out.
sentences.mnemonic: One ending for the group, whatever the verb did to get there.

sentences.cue: Press the button so the door opens

words.note: taḍghaṭ minus ta- leaves ḍghaṭ, two consonants, so the helping i- goes in front. It takes ʿalā: in Arabic you press ON a thing.
z is a sun letter, so the article's l is swallowed: az-zirr, with the r held long.
The purpose li- again, on the he/it-form of this module's first verb. The door is what does the opening, so the verb wears its person.

sentences.trap: "Press the button" has no preposition in English. iḍghaṭ needs ʿalā, and dropping it leaves a verb hanging with nothing to press against.
sentences.sound: IḌ-ghaṭ — the ḍ and ṭ are both emphatic, made with the tongue flat and the sound pushed back, which is what makes the word feel heavy.

variations.cue: Press the button so the manager can come in
variations.changed: the purpose: the door opening → the manager entering

variations.cue: Press the button, then wait
variations.changed: the purpose clause becomes a second step

mistake.why: English's bare object copied across. iḍghaṭ reaches its object through ʿalā, and without it the sentence has the shape of a verb that takes nothing.

sentences.usage: Lifts, machines, forms on a screen — the everyday instruction with a reason attached.
sentences.mnemonic: Two heavy letters, one preposition: press ON it.

sentences.display: lā tadhhab ilā as-sūq qabla al-akl
sentences.script: لا تذهب إلى السوق قبل الأكل
sentences.cue: Don't go to the market before eating
sentences.literal: Not you-go to the-market before the-eating

words.note: The maṣdar of "eat", L3-M1's move again: qabla holds a noun and never a verb, so "before eating" comes out as "before the-eating".

sentences.trap: There is no negative imperative in Arabic to reach for. A prohibition borrows lā plus the you-form of the present, which is the very shape the positive imperative was built by discarding.
sentences.sound: The lā is held — a long a with nothing clipped — and tadhhab keeps its ordinary present shape underneath it.

variations.display: lā tadhhab ilā al-ʿamal qabla al-akl
variations.script: لا تذهب إلى العمل قبل الأكل
variations.cue: Don't go to work before eating
variations.changed: the destination: as-sūq → al-ʿamal

variations.display: lā tadhhab ilā as-sūq qabla an-nawm
variations.script: لا تذهب إلى السوق قبل النوم
variations.cue: Don't go to the market before bed
variations.changed: the noun after qabla: al-akl → an-nawm

mistake.why: A negative bolted onto an imperative, which Arabic does not have. Say lā taftaḥ al-bāb: the prohibition is built on the present, not on the order.

sentences.usage: House rules, warnings on a sign, an instruction with a step you must not skip.
sentences.mnemonic: To forbid, put the prefix back and lā in front.

sentences.cue: Wait here for the manager to come

words.note: A longer verb, and the rule still holds: tantaẓir minus ta- leaves ntaẓir, two consonants, so a helping i- makes intaẓir.
Purpose li- on "come". English needs "wait FOR him TO come", two words; Arabic does it with one li- and the person already on the verb.

sentences.trap: English's "wait for X to come" has a for and a to. Arabic has one li- and no separate word for the person waited on — the yaʾtī is already "he comes".
sentences.sound: in-TA-ẓir, with the ẓ the emphatic partner of dh; the whole word runs into the li- of the next one.

variations.cue: Wait at home for the manager to come
variations.changed: where you wait: hunā → fī al-bayt

variations.cue: Wait here for the manager to come in
variations.changed: the purpose verb: come → come in

mistake.why: English word order pushed through li-. The verb comes straight after li-, and the person it belongs to comes after the verb: li-yaʾtī al-mudīr.

sentences.usage: A counter, a doorway, an office — the instruction plus the reason for standing still.
sentences.mnemonic: One li- covers both the for and the to.

sentences.display: ismaʿ al-mudīr, thumma unẓur ilā al-kitāb
sentences.script: اسمع المدير، ثم انظر إلى الكتاب
sentences.cue: Listen to the manager, then look at the book
sentences.literal: Listen the-manager, then look to the-book

words.note: tasmaʿ minus ta- gives smaʿ, so the helping i- is added. It takes its object bare: in Arabic you listen someone, with no word for "to".
tanẓur minus ta- gives nẓur, and the helping vowel copies the stem's u — so it is unẓur, not inẓur. It reaches its object through ilā.

sentences.trap: The two verbs take the opposite prepositions from English's. ismaʿ wants its object bare where English says "to", and unẓur wants ilā where English says "at".
sentences.sound: IS-maʿ, then UN-ẓur: same shape, different helping vowel, and the difference is only that nẓur carries a u inside it.

variations.cue: Listen to the manager, then say yes
variations.changed: the second step: looking → answering

variations.display: unẓur ilā al-kitāb, thumma ismaʿ al-mudīr
variations.script: انظر إلى الكتاب، ثم اسمع المدير
variations.cue: Look at the book, then listen to the manager
variations.changed: the order of the two steps

mistake.why: English's "listen TO" carried over. ismaʿ takes the person straight: ismaʿ al-mudīr. The ilā belongs to unẓur, in the very next clause.

sentences.usage: Classroom and workplace instructions, and the everyday two-step of attend then check.
sentences.mnemonic: Listen at nothing, look to something.

sentences.cue: Say yes, then open the door

words.note: taqūl loses its ta- and its long ū at once: qul. The endings bring the vowel back — qulī to a woman, qulū to a group.

sentences.trap: The rule predicts something like uqūl. A hollow verb shortens instead, and no amount of reasoning gets you from taqūl to qul — this one is learned.
sentences.sound: qu-LĪ — the q is the deep k made far back, and the long ī at the end is what marks the woman being addressed.

variations.cue: Say yes, then open the door (to a man)
variations.changed: the addressee: both endings drop

variations.cue: Say yes, then open the door (to a group)
variations.changed: the addressee: both endings become -ū

mistake.why: Two orders in one breath to one person, wearing two different endings. Once the addressee is chosen, every imperative in the sentence has to agree with her.

sentences.usage: A short chain of instructions to one person, where the ending is what says which person.
sentences.mnemonic: The vowel qul swallowed comes back the moment an ending arrives.

sentences.display: awwalan, ḍaʿ al-māʾ, thāniyan aḍif as-sukkar
sentences.script: أولًا، ضع الماء، ثانيًا أضف السكر
sentences.cue: First, put in the water, secondly add the sugar
sentences.literal: Firstly, put the-water, secondly add the-sugar

words.note: Second place in a list. It wears the same -an tail as L3-M1's awwalan and akhīran — the ending that turns a word into an adverb.
From tuḍīf. This shape gives aḍif, with a hamza of its own rather than the rule's helping vowel, so it is learned as it stands.

sentences.trap: English can number steps or not, and "first" can sit anywhere. awwalan and thāniyan open their clause and stay there, and once you have started numbering you are expected to finish.
sentences.sound: THĀ-ni-yan, with the th of "think" and the -an tail clipped short — the same tail, said the same way, as awwalan just before it.

variations.display: awwalan, ḍaʿ al-māʾ, thāniyan aḍif al-qahwa
variations.script: أولًا، ضع الماء، ثانيًا أضف القهوة
variations.cue: First, put in the water, secondly add the coffee
variations.changed: the second ingredient: as-sukkar → al-qahwa

variations.display: awwalan, ḍaʿ al-māʾ, thumma aḍif as-sukkar
variations.script: أولًا، ضع الماء، ثم أضف السكر
variations.cue: First, put in the water, then add the sugar
variations.changed: the marker: thāniyan → thumma

mistake.display: al-awwal, ḍaʿ al-māʾ, ath-thānī aḍif as-sukkar
mistake.script: الأول، ضع الماء، الثاني أضف السكر
mistake.why: Those are the adjectives "the first" and "the second", naming things rather than ordering steps. The step markers carry the adverb's -an: awwalan, thāniyan.

sentences.usage: A numbered recipe or procedure — the frame that lets four or five orders arrive without running together.
sentences.mnemonic: The -an is what turns a number into a step.

comprehensionPool.cue: Put the sugar in the coffee
Open the window so the air comes in
Take the bread, all of you
Listen to the manager, then say yes
Open the door so the manager can come in
